hints: Start by thinking about timing - when in life does a female first start meiosis compared to when a male first starts making sperm?
Think about what happens to the cytoplasm in meiosis - how many useful cells result from one primary spermatocyte compared to one primary oocyte?
Think about whether meiosis runs straight through to the end in both sexes, or whether it pauses and needs a trigger to finish in one sex.
walkthrough:
Timing of the start**
In females, oogonia enter meiosis I before birth and then arrest as primary oocytes in prophase I. They stay arrested until puberty and then one at a time resume development. In males, spermatogonia do not enter meiosis until puberty, then produce sperm continuously from then on into old age and in much larger numbers.

Products and continuity of meiosis**
One primary spermatocyte completes meiosis to give four equal haploid spermatids that become sperm. One primary oocyte divides very unequally to give only one large secondary oocyte / ovum plus small polar bodies that degenerate. Female meiosis is also interrupted with long delays, and meiosis II is only completed if fertilisation occurs, while male meiosis runs continuously without interruption.

Final answer: Female gametogenesis begins before birth, male begins at puberty; one ovum produced per meiosis compared to four spermatozoa; female meiosis is interrupted / arrested and only completed after fertilisation, male meiosis is continuous.

hints: Look across Table 4.1 at loci P, Q, R and S and count how many different allele lengths in bp appear at each locus in all the animals listed.
Recall what biological process creates a brand new allele with a different DNA base sequence and length where none existed before.
walkthrough:
Finding the most variable locus**
Count the distinct allele sizes. Locus P has 211, 213, 216 - three alleles. Locus Q has 151, 154 - two alleles. Locus S has 133, 137, 141 - three alleles. Locus R has 188, 190, 200, 206 - four different lengths, so it shows the most genetic variability.

Origin of different allele lengths**
Different alleles with different base-pair lengths arise by mutation, for example insertion, deletion or duplication of DNA bases that alter sequence length. This is the original source of genetic variation.

hints: Remember what heterozygous looks like in this table - the two allele columns for that locus will show two different numbers / different shades.
Scan each individual row by row and note where the two numbers match and where they differ, starting with females A and B and male C.
Do not forget offspring 5, the product of sexual reproduction - check its P, Q, R and S loci for any loci with two different alleles.
walkthrough:
What counts as heterozygous here**
Heterozygous means the two alleles at a locus are different, so you see two different bp values. Homozygous means the same value twice, for example 151/151 or 190/190. Offspring 1-4 are homozygous at all four loci shown.

Applying this to the parents and offspring 5**
Female A has different alleles at P (211 and 216), Q (151 and 154) and R (188 and 200). Female B has different alleles at P (211 and 213) and S (137 and 141). Male C has different alleles at P (211 and 216), Q (151 and 154) and R (188 and 206). Offspring 5, from B x C, has different alleles at P (211 and 216) and R (190 and 206), so all of A, B, C and 5 are heterozygous at one or more loci.

Final answer: Heterozygous animals are female A, female B, male C and offspring 5. A heterozygous at P, Q and R e.g. 211/216 at P; B heterozygous at P and S e.g. 211/213 at P and 137/141 at S; C heterozygous at P, Q and R e.g. 188/206 at R; offspring 5 heterozygous at P and R e.g. 211/216 at P and 190/206 at R.

hints: For the clone idea, compare offspring 1 directly with offspring 2, and offspring 3 directly with offspring 4 - do they have identical allele pairs at every locus?
For the mitosis-only idea, compare each offspring back to its mother - if it were made by mitosis alone, what would you expect its alleles to look like compared to the mother?
walkthrough:
Testing the clone suggestion**
Clones must be genetically identical. Offspring 1 is 216/216 at P, 151/151 at Q, 200/200 at R, while offspring 2 is 211/211 at P, 154/154 at Q, 188/188 at R. They are clearly different. Similarly offspring 3 is 211/211 at P and 141/141 at S, while offspring 4 is 213/213 at P and 137/137 at S. So 1 is not a clone of 2, and 3 is not a clone of 4.

Testing the mitosis-only suggestion**
Mitosis copies the mother exactly, so offspring would be WZ females heterozygous just like the mother. In fact all of offspring 1-4 are ZZ males and homozygous everywhere, and each differs from its mother. For example mother A is 211/216 at P but offspring 1 is 216/216 and offspring 2 is 211/211. This pattern fits meiosis followed by doubling of chromosomes, not simple mitosis.

Final answer: Not clones: offspring 1 and 2 differ at P, Q and R e.g. 216/216 vs 211/211 at P; offspring 3 and 4 differ at P and S e.g. 141/141 vs 137/137 at S. Not mitosis-only asexual: offspring 1 and 2 differ from A at P, Q and R and offspring 3 and 4 differ from B at P and S, whereas mitosis would give offspring genetically identical to mother.

hints: Think about the practical problem of finding a mate when you live on a small island with very few Komodo dragons around.
Think about what it means for survival of the population if a lone female can still produce offspring, and what sex those offspring are in this species.
Think about the genetic cost when offspring come from only one parent with no fertilisation - what happens to variation and heterozygosity?
Link that loss of variation to future risks such as harmful recessive alleles meeting and inability to adapt to disease or environmental change.
walkthrough:
Why reproducing alone helps on an island**
On a small island population mates are rare and a female may never meet a male. Being able to produce viable eggs without a male gives reproductive assurance and keeps the population alive. In Komodo dragons this parthenogenesis produces ZZ males only, so the female can then mate with her own sons in the next generation to return to sexual reproduction. Because there is no new gene mixing, the successful gene combinations already adapted to that island are retained.

Why it is risky in the long term**
The cost is a severe loss of genetic variation. Offspring 1-4 are homozygous at all loci tested, showing decreased heterozygosity and a tiny gene pool. This allows harmful recessive alleles to become homozygous and expressed, giving inbreeding depression and loss of hybrid vigour. With little variation the population cannot evolve to resist new diseases or cope with environmental change, increasing extinction risk.

Final answer: Advantages: mates may be scarce on small islands so female can still reproduce to continue population / species; all offspring are male (ZZ) so female can later mate with sons; retains adaptations to island environment. Disadvantages: reduction in genetic variation / small gene pool with decreased heterozygosity; harmful recessive alleles may come together causing inbreeding depression / loss of hybrid vigour; cannot adapt to changing environment.
